issues.legal_issue: A hereditary service tenure of this kind does not become joint family coparcenary property merely because it has descended through paternal ancestors, and family members do not acquire an interest in it by birth.
material_facts: The disputed lands were Birbhum ghatwali tenures held in connection with an office and the performance of public duties.
The tenure was impartible, generally inalienable, conditional on performance of duties, and liable to forfeiture for misconduct.
The ghatwal for the time being was maintained in exclusive possession, and other family members had no rights over the tenure while it was in his hands.
issues.conclusion: The Mitakshara rule giving sons and other descendants an interest by birth in ancestral property does not apply to Birbhum ghatwali tenures; the family members acquired no coparcenary interest in the tenure.
issues.legal_principle: The nature and incidents of the tenure displace the Mitakshara birthright rule: an office-linked tenure held in exclusive possession, impartible and conditional on service, lacks the community of interest and unity of possession characteristic of coparcenary property. The Court relied on Regulation XXIX of 1814 and on Katama Natchir v. The Raja of Sivaganga, Kali Pershad v. Anand Roy, Chhatradhari Singh v. Saraswati Kumari, Raja Durga Prashad Singh v. Tribeni Singh, and Narayan Singh v. Niranjan Chakravarti. It distinguished the principles governing impartible estates that are otherwise established to be joint family property.

predicates.birbhum_service_tenure_case: The succession dispute concerns a hereditary service tenure of the Birbhum ghatwali kind.
predicates.tenure_attached_to_service_office: The holder possesses the tenure in connection with an office and duties to be performed for the grantor or public authority.
predicates.holder_has_exclusive_possession: The holder for the time being possesses the tenure exclusively, with no rights in it held by other family members.
predicates.tenure_is_impartible: The tenure is not divisible among the holder's heirs.

issues.definition: When a Birbhum-type hereditary service tenure is held exclusively, is attached to an office, and is impartible, family members do not acquire an interest in it by birth.

issues.legal_issue: A widow may succeed to a Birbhum ghatwali tenure ahead of the nearest male agnate when the holder dies without direct descendants, even if the family is joint.
material_facts: The deceased holder left a widow and no issue or direct male descendants.
Evidence showed thirteen instances in the relevant clan in which a widow succeeded to a ghatwali tenure in preference to a male agnate.
No instance was proved in which a female was excluded because an agnate claimed as a coparcener by survivorship.
The Government representative recognized the widow by reference to an established precedent of recognizing a widow in the absence of a direct heir.
issues.conclusion: The widow was entitled to succeed in preference to the nearest male agnate even if the family was joint, and the appeal against her succession was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Custom and usage can govern or modify succession to ghatwali property; repeated instances of tacit and unquestioned application may establish a customary rule. Regulation XXIX of 1814 does not prescribe a rule of succession, and its use of “descendants” does not exclude a widow who is an heir under personal law or custom. The Court relied on the succession evidence and distinguished Fulbati Kumari v. Maheshwari Prasad, which expressly did not concern Birbhum ghatwali tenures; it also referred to Raja Durga Prashad Singh v. Tribeni Singh on the absence of family rights over the tenure while held by the ghatwal.

predicates.customary_instances_support_widow_succes: Past succession practice in the relevant community included widows succeeding ahead of male agnates, without proof of exclusion on a survivorship claim.

issues.definition: If a holder of a Birbhum-type service tenure dies without direct descendants, leaves a widow, and the customary succession practice supports widows succeeding ahead of male agnates, the widow takes ahead of the nearest male agnate.

issues.legal_issue: A Birbhum ghatwali tenure that is heritable from generation to generation does not revert to the grantor merely because its holder dies.
material_facts: The governing regulation provided that the ghatwals and their descendants were to be maintained in possession from generation to generation, subject to payment and performance conditions.
The appellant argued that the tenure reverted to the grantor at the holder's death and was notionally granted anew to the next holder.
The grantor's powers to dismiss a holder or forfeit the tenure arose in specified circumstances such as misconduct or failure to perform obligations.
issues.conclusion: The tenure did not revert to the grantor at each holder's death; it vested in the next heir when succession opened.
issues.legal_principle: A tenure expressly heritable from generation to generation cannot be treated as terminating and being regranted at every death; inheritance does not remain in abeyance. Regulation XXIX of 1814 and its provisions for continued possession, together with the tenure's hereditary character, support that conclusion.

predicates.hereditary_service_tenure_case: The dispute concerns a hereditary service tenure.
predicates.tenure_passes_generation_to_generation: The tenure is held under an arrangement providing for continued possession through successive generations, subject to its conditions.
predicates.holder_died: The person holding the tenure died and succession to it opened.

issues.definition: When a holder dies during a tenure that passes through successive generations, the tenure does not automatically revert to the grantor.

issues.legal_issue: Property acquired by a predecessor through a decree and inherited by the holder is separate property when no descendant acquires an interest in it by birth, so the holder's widow may inherit it.
material_facts: Some of the disputed items were acquired by the holder's father through a court decree against a collateral who claimed them as heir to a previous owner.
The holder inherited those items from his father and died without a son who could acquire an interest in them by birth.
The parties accepted that the widow would inherit if the property was the holder's separate property.
issues.conclusion: The items were separate property in the holder's hands, and the widow was entitled to inherit them; the male claimant had no birthright claim to them.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara principles, property acquired by obstructed heritage is separate property in the recipient's hands; absent a son acquiring an interest by birth, the widow succeeds as heir. The Court applied this reasoning to the items acquired by decree and then inherited by the last holder.

predicates.property_acquired_by_predecessor_through: A predecessor acquired the property through a court decree in a dispute with a collateral claimant.
predicates.holder_inherited_property: The deceased holder received the property by inheritance from that predecessor.
predicates.no_descendant_acquired_birthright_intere: No descendant of the holder acquired an interest in the property by birth before the holder's death.

issues.definition: If a predecessor obtains property by decree, the holder inherits it, and no descendant acquires an interest by birth, the widow inherits it as the holder's separate property.
